verses.text: Saul spoke to Jonathan his son, and to all his servants, that they should kill David. But Jonathan, Saul’s son, greatly delighted in David.
Jonathan told David, saying, “Saul my father seeks to kill you. Now therefore, please take care of yourself in the morning, and live in a secret place, and hide yourself.
I will go out and stand beside my father in the field where you are, and I will talk with my father about you; and if I see anything, I will tell you.”

Jonathan spoke good of David to Saul his father, and said to him, “Don’t let the king sin against his servant, against David; because he has not sinned against you, and because his works have been very good toward you;

for he put his life in his hand, and struck the Philistine, and Yahweh worked a great victory for all Israel. You saw it, and rejoiced. Why then will you sin against innocent blood, to kill David without a cause?”
Saul listened to the voice of Jonathan: and Saul swore, “As Yahweh lives, he shall not be put to death.”
Jonathan called David, and Jonathan showed him all those things. Then Jonathan brought David to Saul, and he was in his presence, as before.
There was war again. David went out, and fought with the Philistines, and killed them with a great slaughter; and they fled before him.
An evil spirit from Yahweh was on Saul, as he sat in his house with his spear in his hand; and David was playing with his hand.
Saul sought to pin David to the wall with the spear; but he slipped away out of Saul’s presence, and he stuck the spear into the wall. David fled, and escaped that night.
Saul sent messengers to David’s house, to watch him, and to kill him in the morning. Michal, David’s wife, told him, saying, “If you don’t save your life tonight, tomorrow you will be killed.”
So Michal let David down through the window. He went away, fled, and escaped.
Michal took the teraphim,  and laid it in the bed, and put a pillow of goats’ hair at its head, and covered it with clothes.
When Saul sent messengers to take David, she said, “He is sick.”
Saul sent the messengers to see David, saying, “Bring him up to me in the bed, that I may kill him.”
When the messengers came in, behold, the teraphim was in the bed, with the pillow of goats’ hair at its head.
Saul said to Michal, “Why have you deceived me thus, and let my enemy go, so that he is escaped?” Michal answered Saul, “He said to me, ‘Let me go! Why should I kill you?’”
Now David fled and escaped, and came to Samuel at Ramah, and told him all that Saul had done to him. He and Samuel went and lived in Naioth.
Saul was told, saying, “Behold, David is at Naioth in Ramah.”

Saul sent messengers to seize David: and when they saw the company of the prophets prophesying, and Samuel standing as head over them, God’s Spirit came on Saul’s messengers, and they also prophesied.
When Saul was told, he sent other messengers, and they also prophesied. Saul sent messengers again the third time, and they also prophesied.
Then he also went to Ramah, and came to the great well that is in Secu: and he asked, “Where are Samuel and David?” One said, “Behold, they are at Naioth in Ramah.”
He went there to Naioth in Ramah. Then God’s Spirit came on him also, and he went on, and prophesied, until he came to Naioth in Ramah.
He also stripped off his clothes, and he also prophesied before Samuel, and lay down naked all that day and all that night. Therefore they say, “Is Saul also among the prophets?”

footnotes.content: Fear and envy make a tyrant speak murder casually. Saul's orders ripple out like poison from a poisoned heart—yet notice Jonathan is named here first, and his delight in David stands as a quiet wall against his father's rage. Love is stronger than command.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan moves at once—not to obey Saul, but to save David. This is covenant-love in action: risking his own standing to warn his friend. When you hear 'take care of yourself,' you hear someone who loves you enough to act.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan's plan is both humble and brave—he'll go into the field beside his father and speak. He doesn't know if it will work, but he is determined to try. This is what loyalty looks like: showing up, standing beside, and speaking what is true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan appeals not to sentiment but to Saul's own memory: David has not sinned against you. He reminds his father of what is plainly true. When we plead for another's life, it is often plain truth, spoken calmly, that carries the weight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan invokes Goliath—the victory that Saul saw and rejoiced over. He shows Saul the mirror: this man you wish to kill is the very man God used to deliver you and all Israel. The cross-reference is unmistakable, and for a moment, it stops Saul's hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul listens. Jonathan's steady voice reaches something in his father that fury had locked away. Saul swears by Yahweh's life—the greatest oath—that David will not die. For now, the storm passes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan brings David back to the palace, back into Saul's house as if nothing had changed. This is the power of intercession—a true friend speaks and doors open again, at least for a time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: War returns, and David goes out once more to fight the Philistines with great slaughter. He gives everything in service to Saul's kingdom, never knowing it is the very faithfulness that will enrage the king.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An evil spirit from Yahweh is on Saul—Scripture speaks plainly of God permitting it. Saul sits in his own house, spear in hand, while David plays. The contrast is stark: one man restless with darkness, the other offering music and comfort.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul hurls his spear to pin David to the wall—a murder attempt in his own house. But the Lord opens a gap between intention and deed. David slips away, the spear stays in the wall, and by nightfall, he is gone. Providence often works through narrow margins.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul sends watchers to David's house to kill him by morning. But Michal, David's wife, has ears and a heart. She hears the danger and speaks urgently to her husband—another woman who loves wisely and acts fast.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Michal lets David down through the window in the night. There is no hesitation here, no divided loyalty between husband and father. She chooses to save him, and he escapes into darkness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Michal takes the teraphim—a household idol—and places it in the bed to deceive the guards. The teraphim was kept in David's own house; its presence here shows he had begun to settle, to believe he was safe. Michal's quick wit gives him a few more hours.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Michal tells Saul's messengers that David is sick and cannot rise. A small lie spoken to buy time and save a life—sometimes the righteous act is not the obvious one, but the necessary one.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul is not satisfied with the report. He commands the messengers to bring David on his very bed so he can kill him there. The king's murderous intent now turns toward his own house and his own son's wife—his paranoia has no limits.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The messengers enter and find only the teraphim in the bed. Michal's deception has held just long enough. David is already beyond pursuit, beyond the reach of Saul's murderous hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul confronts Michal with rage. She answers quickly, invoking David's threat against her own life—a lie that protects them both. Michal has placed herself between a tyrant and his prey, and she pays no price she cannot bear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David flees to Samuel at Ramah and tells him all. He comes to a prophet, a man who hears God's voice. Together they go to Naioth—a place of refuge near a man of God. The hunted find shelter near someone who knows the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul is told David is at Naioth in Ramah, and he acts without delay. His jealous anger knows no rest. He will hunt David to the gates of a prophet's house, never understanding that some places are guarded by a hand higher than any king's.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul sends soldiers to seize David, but when they see the company of prophets prophesying and Samuel standing at their head, God's Spirit falls on the soldiers themselves. Suddenly they are not hunters but worshippers. The Lord's presence changes everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul sends again and again—three times his soldiers go out to capture David, and three times they are caught up in prophecy and cannot lay a hand on him. The king's will meets a wall it cannot break through. God is simply standing in the way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul himself goes to the great well in Secu and asks where Samuel and David are. The king is now personally hunting. Yet even his own journey will not end as he plans.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul arrives at Naioth, and God's Spirit comes on him also—the persecutor becomes the prophesier. He goes on prophesying all the way to Naioth. I've watched this pattern in my own life: sometimes what we pursue most relentlessly is exactly where the Lord will meet us and turn us inside out.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul strips off his clothes and prophesies naked, day and night. The people say, 'Is Saul also among the prophets?'—a question that echoes throughout Israel. The mighty king lies undone by the Spirit of God, while David remains sheltered and hidden. There is an upside-down kingdom at work here.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
